notes.title: Is this digoxin toxicity? What do you do?

lines.text: An older patient with heart failure or atrial fibrillation takes digoxin, usually together with a diuretic such as furosemide. New symptoms, a slow pulse or a low potassium mean danger.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance → digoxin toxicity.
New irregular rhythm or a slow pulse → toxicity reaching the heart.
Patient also on furosemide or a thiazide → expect LOW potassium.
Low K⁺ → a NORMAL dose becomes toxic. High Ca²⁺ does the same.
Low magnesium also raises toxicity.
Quinidine or verapamil added recently → digoxin level rises.
Amiodarone also raises digoxin levels.
Before every dose, count the apical pulse for one full minute; hold the dose if it is below 60 in an adult and report.
Signs of toxicity → hold digoxin (and the diuretic) and report.
Check serum K⁺, Ca²⁺ and the digoxin level; correct the electrolytes.
Slow heart rate → atropine. Arrhythmia → lidocaine. Severe toxicity → digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).
Digoxin blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump → more calcium inside heart cells → stronger beat. It also slows the heart through the vagus nerve.
Digoxin binds the pump's potassium site. Less K⁺ in the blood leaves more sites free for digoxin, so its effect grows.
“The dose was too low”: the dose didn't change, the potassium dropped.
“Give the scheduled dose” when the pulse is slow and vision has changed: never.
“Increase the furosemide”: it lowers potassium further and worsens toxicity.
Usual dose: 0.125–0.5 mg by mouth daily.
Hold if apical pulse < 60/min (adult).
Therapeutic serum level: about 0.5–2 ng/ml.
A 70-year-old man with heart failure takes digoxin and furosemide. He reports nausea and seeing yellow halos. Pulse 54/min, irregular. Serum K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
a. Give the morning digoxin dose as scheduled ✗: signs of toxicity, pulse below 60.
b. Hold digoxin and report; check potassium and digoxin level ✓
c. Increase the furosemide to relieve heart failure ✗: lowers K⁺ further.
d. Reassure him that nausea is a common, harmless effect ✗: nausea is an early toxicity sign.

notes.title: Choosing a BP drug for the patient in front of you

lines.text: A hypertensive patient with one extra detail: pregnancy, diabetes, a cough on treatment, asthma, an enlarged prostate, gout, or an emergency. That detail decides the drug.
No other disease (in Ethiopia) → start amlodipine; add a thiazide; third, an ACE inhibitor.
Pregnant → methyldopa, nifedipine (modified release), or a β-blocker in the third trimester.
Pregnant → NEVER ACE inhibitors, ARBs or thiazides.
Severe hypertension or crisis in pregnancy → IV labetalol or IV hydralazine; seizures in pre-eclampsia → magnesium sulfate.
Diabetes or kidney disease → ACE inhibitor (protects the kidneys).
Dry cough on an ACE inhibitor → switch to an ARB (losartan).
Asthma or COPD → avoid non-selective β-blockers (propranolol).
Enlarged prostate (BPH) → α1-blocker (prazosin).
Gout → avoid thiazides (they raise uric acid).
Hypertensive emergency → IV sodium nitroprusside (protect from light).
ACE inhibitor + spironolactone or K⁺ supplements → dangerous hyperkalemia.
Stopping clonidine suddenly → rebound hypertensive crisis; taper over 2–4 days.
Angioedema on an ACE inhibitor → stop it; never restart.
Black patients respond better to diuretics and CCBs than to ACE inhibitors or β-blockers.
A 32-year-old woman at 24 weeks of pregnancy has BP 150/100 mmHg. She has been taking lisinopril since before pregnancy. What is the most appropriate change?
a. Continue lisinopril at the same dose ✗: ACE inhibitors harm the fetus.
b. Switch to methyldopa ✓: the preferred BP drug in pregnancy.
c. Add hydrochlorothiazide ✗: thiazides are avoided in pregnancy.
d. Switch to losartan ✗: ARBs are also contraindicated in pregnancy.
A 56-year-old diabetic on enalapril has had a dry, tickly cough for a month. Most appropriate action? → switch to an ARB such as losartan.
A farmer, or someone who drank insecticide, arrives with too much acetylcholine everywhere: wet, slow and small.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Insecticide exposure (malathion, parathion, diazinon) → organophosphate.
Salivation, tearing, sweating, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, wheeze and secretions in the airway → muscarinic overload.
Pinpoint pupils + slow heart rate → acetylcholine excess, not an opioid, when the patient is also wet and sweating.
Muscle twitching then weakness → nicotinic effect at the muscles.
Airway first: suction secretions, give oxygen, support breathing.
Decontaminate: remove clothes, wash skin; reduce further absorption.
Give atropine, the cornerstone of treatment, and repeat it until secretions dry.
Give pralidoxime (2-PAM) early, before the enzyme “ages”.
Organophosphates bind acetylcholinesterase permanently, so acetylcholine builds up at every synapse.
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors (the wet, slow signs). Pralidoxime frees the enzyme, but only before aging.
Neostigmine or physostigmine: they also block cholinesterase → would make it worse.
Naloxone because the pupils are pinpoint: wrong; opioids don't cause salivation, sweating and diarrhea.
Adrenaline: for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, not cholinergic poisoning.
A 40-year-old farmer is brought in 1 hour after spraying insecticide. He is drooling, sweating and wheezing, with pinpoint pupils. Pulse 48/min. Which drug is the priority?
a. Atropine ✓: blocks the excess acetylcholine; the cornerstone of treatment.
b. Neostigmine ✗: another cholinesterase inhibitor; makes it worse.
c. Adrenaline ✗: not for cholinergic poisoning.
d. Naloxone ✗: reverses opioids; this picture is cholinergic.

notes.title: A TB patient with a new complaint: which drug, what to do

lines.text: A patient on TB treatment (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) comes with a new symptom. Match the symptom to the drug, then act.
Burning or numb feet and hands → isoniazid neuropathy → give pyridoxine (vitamin B6).
Orange urine, sweat or tears → rifampin; harmless, reassure and explain.
Blurred vision or trouble telling red from green → ethambutol; report.
Joint pain, high uric acid, gout → pyrazinamide.
Jaundice, dark urine, loss of appetite → hepatitis from isoniazid, rifampin or pyrazinamide; report.
Woman on the pill starts rifampin → contraceptive failure; she needs another method.
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears on an injectable (streptomycin, amikacin, capreomycin) → ototoxicity; report.
Isoniazid causes a relative B6 deficiency, more in slow acetylators, malnutrition, alcoholism, diabetes and AIDS.
Rifampin strongly induces liver enzymes, so many drugs (pills, anticoagulants, HIV drugs) are cleared faster.
“Stop all TB drugs” for orange urine: wrong; it's expected and harmless.
Treating TB with one drug: resistance develops quickly; always several drugs.
Ethambutol in a child too young to report vision changes: avoided.
A 35-year-old man with diabetes has been on TB treatment for 6 weeks. He complains of burning and numbness in both feet. What is the most appropriate intervention?
a. Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as ordered ✓: isoniazid neuropathy; diabetes raises the risk.
b. Stop all TB drugs immediately ✗: neuropathy is managed with B6, not by stopping treatment.
c. Reassure him that it's caused by rifampin ✗: rifampin causes orange fluids, not neuropathy.
d. Check his color vision ✗: that's for ethambutol.
A woman on the combined pill starts TB treatment. What should the nurse teach? → rifampin can make the pill fail; use an additional or different method.
A woman asks for family planning. One detail about her (breastfeeding, days since delivery, smoking, an illness, another drug) decides which method is safe.
Breastfeeding → progestin-only (mini pill, injection, implant). No combined (estrogen) methods.
Postpartum, NOT breastfeeding, less than 21 days after delivery → still no estrogen (clot risk is high); progestin-only methods are safe.
Over 35 AND smoking → no combined method; choose progestin-only.
Migraine, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, past clot, liver disease, heart failure → no combined method.
Fibroids → mini pill rather than combined pill.
On rifampin, phenytoin or phenobarbital → the pill may fail; add or switch to another method.
Wants 3 months of protection without daily pills → depot medroxyprogesterone injection, 150 mg IM every 3 months.
Unprotected sex: within 72 hours → levonorgestrel-based pills; up to 120 hours → mifepristone ± misoprostol.
Combined methods contain estrogen, which raises the risk of thromboembolism and hypertension.
Progestin-only methods avoid estrogen's side effects, but have a slightly higher failure rate.
Combined pill or combined vaginal ring for a woman 2 weeks after delivery: both contain estrogen → wrong before 21 days.
Female sterilization for a young woman who only wants spacing: permanent → not “most appropriate”.
Ectopic pregnancy or nausea, weight gain and low mood in a woman on the pill → progestin side effects.
Thromboembolism in a woman on the pill → estrogen.
A 28-year-old multiparous woman is 14 days postpartum and not breastfeeding. She has no chronic disease. What is the most appropriate contraceptive method?
a. Progestin-only injectable ✓: safe right after delivery, no estrogen.
b. Combined oral contraceptive ✗: estrogen before 21 days postpartum.
c. Female sterilization ✗: permanent; nothing suggests she wants that.
d. Combined vaginal ring ✗: also contains estrogen.
A woman's condom tore 4 days (96 hours) ago. Most appropriate emergency option? → mifepristone (works up to 120 hours). Levonorgestrel-based pills are for up to 72 hours.
